Weather Intelligence for the Modern Warfighter

Feb 19, 2018 BY ERIC WEBSTER

High in the sky, a fighter jet links up with an aerial refueling tanker and then streaks toward its target as clouds build ahead. At sea, high winds and reduced visibility force a swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles to abort landing on a waiting aircraft carrier. On the ground, a convoy of autonomous trucks carrying fuel, ammunition, and supplies takes fire as a line of intense thunderstorms quickly approaches. Meanwhile, in cyberspace, thousands of enemy hackers launch a coordinated attack on critical ground systems processing massive volumes of weather, navigation, and surveillance data essential to conducting intelligence operations.

This once futuristic vision of joint military operations “from mud to sun,” with combat taking place on both the physical and virtual battlefields, is fast becoming a reality. More than ever, mission success in this modern battlespace will rely heavily on accurate, detailed, and secure satellite weather data and precision forecasts delivered to the warfighter on time, every time.

To meet its global weather monitoring needs, Department of Defense (DoD) military operations have depended on the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) for the past six decades. While much has changed since the first DMSP satellite was launched—primarily to predict cloud cover in support of America’s first photo reconnaissance satellite program—the importance of assured weather intelligence has remained the same.

Now, as the last DMSP satellites on orbit approach their end of life, the DoD is transitioning to the future Weather System Follow-on (WSF) program. Having supported the DMSP program for more than 50 years, Harris is now developing the next generation of weather systems to help ensure the U.S. and its allies maintain a competitive advantage in today’s multi-theater, multi-threat environment.

THE FUTURE OF WEATHER MONITORING

The ability to gather and quickly deliver accurate and detailed data is critical to successful military operations, the safety of our warfighters, and the protection of mission-critical equipment. Any delay can be the difference between mission success and failure. Focused on core DoD weather requirements such as cloud characterization and theater weather imagery, WSF is poised to benefit from recent advancements in the detail, clarity, and timeliness of weather sensing technology.

For example, our Enhanced Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (E-AVHRR)—developed in partnership with the U.S. Air Force, and built on the legacy of 19 polar-orbiting imagers for the United States and Europe—improves the quality of global weather imagery by providing more channels than its predecessor, while minimizing cost and risk. The additional channels are optimized for improved cloud characterization and can be used to detect aerosols, dust, land-water boundaries, vegetation, snow and ice, hurricanes, and hot spots.

We are also investing in smaller sensors for a future where constellations of smaller, more agile satellites will make our military more resilient to increasingly sophisticated enemy attacks. These instruments, which can fit on small satellites or cubesats, use hyperspectral technology to meet a wide range of mission requirements for the defense, civil, and commercial markets. They are enabled by the miniaturization of sounding and imaging components already proven on orbit, such as on the Harris-built Cross-track Infrared Sounder (CrIS) and Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI).

The CrIS instrument, the second of which recently launched on NOAA’s first Joint Polar Satellite System satellite (JPSS-1), observes more than 2,000 spectral channels to produce three-dimensional profiles of temperature and moisture with high vertical resolution. Studies have shown that CrIS and other hyperspectral infrared sounders improve the accuracy of weather forecast models more than any other type of data.

ABI is the primary instrument on NOAA’s newest generation of Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES), the GOES-R Series. With more channels, higher resolution, and faster refresh than previous GOES imagers, ABI enables earlier and more accurate severe storm warnings, improved hurricane tracking, enhanced detection of fires and hot spots, and closer monitoring of sea ice and dust storms. In some cases, ABI has shown it can detect where thunderstorms will develop before their clouds have even formed.

Innovation by industry has now made it possible to package these advanced capabilities into smaller sensors and satellites requiring less power and lower launch costs. Our focus is to maintain the high performance and data quality from our larger sensors, while offering more affordable and flexible options to meet evolving customer requirements.

EVOLVING TO ENTERPRISE GROUND SERVICES

Reliable ground systems and rapid data processing are just as important to mission success as the instruments collecting the data. After decades of creating a standalone ground system for each new satellite mission, the Air Force is now modernizing and consolidating its ground infrastructure through an initiative known as Enterprise Ground Services (EGS). The goal is a government-owned common ground architecture for command and control of multiple missions ranging from weather to missile defense, enabling enhanced data exploitation and increased efficiency, security, and resiliency.

Serving as a state-of-the-art model for enterprise ground architectures is the GOES-R Ground System, built and fielded by Harris. The GOES-R Ground System provides command and control for NOAA’s new GOES-R series of satellites, produces weather products in less than 30 seconds, and generates space weather products in less than two seconds. The scalable system can process more than 30 terabytes of data per day from multiple instruments, satellites, and orbits; has a storage capacity of 1.4 petabytes; meets high-availability requirements with less than four seconds of downtime per year; and exceeds federal security controls for high-impact systems.

Today, Harris is leveraging enterprise ground expertise to help the Air Force realize its EGS vision. We are providing end-to-end systems engineering and developing mission-unique software utilizing the EGS infrastructure to deliver mission-critical data to support the warfighter. As we continue to improve and innovate, we are making significant research and development investments to advance key enablers of enterprise ground systems, including high-performance computing for fast processing of big data, cloud processing to reduce hardware footprints, machine learning for data exploitation, and cybersecurity to protect critical systems.

Building on more than five decades of designing, developing, and implementing advanced satellite sensors and ground systems for the civil and defense communities, our latest innovations in sensor and ground technologies can help the DoD achieve its objectives for the next generation of military space and ground infrastructure. Ultimately, it’s all about collecting, processing, and delivering accurate and detailed data, quickly and securely, with high-performing, cost-effective, and low-risk solutions.

Eric Webster is vice president of business development, Environmental Solutions, within Harris Corporation's Space and Intelligence Systems segment. Through ongoing support for DMSP, GOES, and other mission-critical satellite programs, Harris has led the industry in advanced technologies for collecting, receiving, and processing weather and environmental information from remote sensing systems.
